title: Exponents, square roots and scientific notation
blurb: Use the exponent rules, find and estimate square roots, and move between standard form and scientific notation.
question: A lab report lists a bacterial count of 3.6 × 10⁵ cells per mL and a particle 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ mm wide. What are these numbers in standard form, and why does one exponent make the number big and the other make it tiny?

teach.body: Formally, aⁿ means n factors of a multiplied together (the base a, the exponent n), a square root √a is the nonnegative number whose square is a, and scientific notation writes a number as c × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ c < 10. In plain English: an exponent counts how many times you multiply, a square root asks "what times itself makes this?", and scientific notation is shorthand for very big or very small numbers.

In words
Example
teach.caption: The rules need the SAME base. A negative exponent makes a fraction, never a negative number.

items: 2³ × 2²: same base, add exponents: 2⁵ = 32. Check the long way: 8 × 4 = 32. ✓
4⁰ + 3¹ = 1 + 3 = 4 (any nonzero number to the 0 is 1; to the 1 is itself).
√50 is not a perfect square. Find the neighbors: 49 < 50 < 64, so 7 < √50 < 8.
50 is much closer to 49 than to 64, so √50 is just above 7 (about 7.07). Check: 7.07² ≈ 49.98. ✓

teach.body: Write one nonzero digit before the decimal point, then × 10 to the number of places the point moved. A positive exponent means a large number (point moves right to expand it): 4.2 × 10³ = 4,200. A negative exponent means a number smaller than 1 (point moves left): 6 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.0006. Multiplying uses the product rule: (3 × 10⁴)(2 × 10³) = 6 × 10⁷.

steps.label: Move point 4 right
steps.sub: until one nonzero digit is in front: 5.2

teach.text: Exponent slips that become TEAS distractors: 2³ is 8, not 2 × 3 = 6; 2⁻³ is 1/8, not −8; 3² × 3⁴ is 3⁶, not 3⁸ (exponents add, not multiply) and not 9⁶ (bases stay the same); and 10⁻⁴ makes a number SMALLER, so its point moves left.

teach.h: Scenario: Rosa reads a lab report
teach.body: Rosa Martinez, a nursing applicant working as a lab assistant, sees a count of 3.6 × 10⁵ cells per mL. Positive exponent, so move the point 5 places right: 360,000 cells per mL. A particle measures 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ mm. Negative exponent, so move the point 4 places left: 0.00012 mm. Check: 360,000 has its first digit in the hundred-thousands place (10⁵); 0.00012 has its first nonzero digit in the ten-thousandths place (10⁻⁴). ✓

items: Same base: multiply → add exponents; divide → subtract; power of a power → multiply.
a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ (a fraction, not a negative).
Know perfect squares to 225; estimate other roots between neighboring perfect squares.
Scientific notation: c × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ c < 10; positive n is big, negative n is small.

summary: You can now apply the exponent rules, including zero and negative exponents, find perfect square roots and estimate the rest, and convert between standard form and scientific notation. You know the add-versus-multiply and negative-exponent slips the TEAS uses.

A.why: Same base: add then subtract exponents: 4 + 2 − 3 = 3, so 3³ = 27. Check: 81 × 9 ÷ 27 = 729 ÷ 27 = 27.

whyNot.0: 243 = 3⁵ multiplies the first two exponents (4 × 2 = 8) and then subtracts 3.
whyNot.2: 9 = 3² divides the exponents (6 ÷ 3) instead of subtracting them.
whyNot.3: 729 = 9³ multiplies the bases; with the same base, the base stays 3.

A.q: A bacterium is about 0.000035 m long. Which is its length in scientific notation?
A.why: Move the point 5 places right to get 3.5. The number is smaller than 1, so the exponent is negative: 3.5 × 10⁻⁵. Check: 3.5 ÷ 100,000 = 0.000035.

whyNot.0: A positive exponent makes a large number: 3.5 × 10⁵ = 350,000.
whyNot.1: 3.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.00035, ten times too big; the point moves 5 places, not 4.
whyNot.3: 3.5 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.0000035, ten times too small; it counts 6 places.

A.q: Between which two consecutive whole numbers does √130 lie?

whyNot.0: 10² = 100 and 11² = 121, both less than 130, so √130 is above 11.
whyNot.1: 12² = 144 is already more than 130, so √130 is below 12.
whyNot.2: 65 is 130 ÷ 2; a square root is not half the number.

B.why: A negative exponent means the reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8.

whyNot.1: −8 makes the answer negative; a negative exponent gives a reciprocal, not a negative number.
whyNot.2: −6 multiplies the base by the exponent: 2 × (−3).
whyNot.3: 1/6 takes the reciprocal of 2 × 3 instead of 2³.

B.why: Multiply coefficients: 4 × 6 = 24. Add exponents: 3 + 5 = 8. So 24 × 10⁸. Make the coefficient less than 10: 2.4 × 10⁹.

whyNot.0: 2.4 × 10⁸ moves the point in 24 but forgets to add 1 to the exponent.
whyNot.1: 2.4 × 10¹⁶ multiplies the exponents (3 × 5 = 15) instead of adding them.
whyNot.3: 10 × 10⁸ adds the coefficients (4 + 6) instead of multiplying them.

B.why: Exponents and roots first: 2³ = 8 and √36 = 6. Multiply: 8 × 6 = 48. Add: 5 + 48 = 53.

C.why: Power of a power: (2³)² = 2⁶. Then 2⁶ × 2⁻⁴ = 2⁶⁺⁽⁻⁴⁾ = 2² = 4. Check: 64 × 1/16 = 4.

whyNot.0: 2 adds the exponents in (2³)² to get 2⁵; a power of a power multiplies them.
whyNot.2: 1,024 = 2¹⁰ subtracts the −4 (6 − (−4)) as if dividing; multiplying adds the exponents.
whyNot.3: −1,024 treats 2⁻⁴ as −16, but a negative exponent gives 1/16, not a negative number.

C.q: Normal saline contains 9 × 10⁻³ g of sodium chloride per mL. How many grams of sodium chloride are in a 500 mL bag?

whyNot.0: 45 g uses 0.09 g per mL, moving the point only 2 places for 10⁻³.
whyNot.1: 0.45 g uses 0.0009 g per mL, moving the point 4 places for 10⁻³.
whyNot.3: 450 g uses 0.9 g per mL, ignoring most of the negative exponent.

whyNot.0: √64 + √36 = 8 + 6 = 14, but √100 = 10. Square roots of a sum can't be split.
whyNot.1: (−5)² = (−5)(−5) = 25; the parentheses include the negative in the square.
whyNot.2: Any nonzero number to the power 0 equals 1, so 10⁰ = 1.

reteach.title: Exponents are doubling bacteria
reteach.question: One bacterium splits into two every 20 minutes. How many are there after 5 splits, and how does that picture explain exponents and roots?

blocks.body: After 1 split there are 2 bacteria, after 2 splits 2 × 2 = 4, after 3 splits 8. After 5 splits: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2⁵ = 32, not 2 × 5 = 10. The exponent counts the splits. A square root runs a square backward: 144 floor tiles laid in a perfect square must be 12 tiles per side, so √144 = 12.

items: 3 splits, then 2 more: 2³ × 2² = 2⁵. Splits add up, so exponents add.
Going back 2 splits from 2⁵: 2⁵ ÷ 2² = 2³. Undoing splits subtracts.
Before any split there is 1 bacterium: 2⁰ = 1.

blocks.text: 5 splits gives 2⁵ = 32 bacteria, not 10. The exponent counts multiplications, it is never a multiplier.

explain.body: Any nonzero number to the power 0 is 1. A negative exponent means the reciprocal: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. So 4⁻¹ = 1/4, a positive fraction.

head: Power of 4
Value
explain.caption: Each step down the table divides by 4.

whyNot.1: 1/4 treats 4⁰ as 0; any nonzero number to the 0 is 1.

explain.body: With the same base: multiplying adds exponents, dividing subtracts them, and raising a power to a power multiplies them. The base never changes.

test.why: Same base, dividing: subtract exponents: 8 − 2 = 6, so 10⁶ (1,000,000).

whyNot.0: 10⁴ divides the exponents (8 ÷ 2) instead of subtracting.
whyNot.2: 10¹⁰ adds the exponents, which is the rule for multiplying.
whyNot.3: 1⁶ divides the bases (10 ÷ 10); the base stays 10.

explain.body: Find the perfect squares on either side. √75: 64 < 75 < 81, so between 8 and 9. 75 is closer to 81 (6 away) than to 64 (11 away), so the root is a little over 8.5.

test.q: Which is the best estimate of √75?
test.why: 64 < 75 < 81, so √75 is between 8 and 9, nearer 9. Check: 8.7² = 75.69, very close to 75.

whyNot.0: 7.5 just moves the decimal point in 75; 7.5² = 56.25.
whyNot.1: 9.3 is above 9, but 9² = 81 is already more than 75; 9.3² = 86.49.
whyNot.3: 37.5 is half of 75; a square root is not half the number.

explain.body: Positive exponent: move the point that many places right (a big number). Negative exponent: move it left (a small number). Fill gaps with zeros.

whyNot.3: 0.000602 moves the point left, which is what 10⁻⁴ would do.
